---
title: "U-Net"
description: "An encoder-decoder convolutional neural network with skip connections, commonly used for image segmentation."
term: "U-Net"
letter: "U"
category: "Computer Vision"
difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

U-Net is a neural-network architecture that labels pixels in an image.
Its encoder learns increasingly abstract features while reducing spatial
resolution; its decoder restores resolution to produce a pixel-level
prediction.

## Technical explanation

The original U-Net uses a contracting path of convolution and downsampling
and an expanding path of upsampling and convolution. Skip connections
concatenate or otherwise combine corresponding encoder features with
decoder features, helping preserve localization information.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

U-Net is widely used for biomedical and other image-segmentation tasks,
particularly when annotated data is limited. Variants adapt it to different
modalities, dimensions, and compute budgets.

## How it works

The encoder builds feature maps at multiple scales. The decoder upsamples
coarse representations, combines them with high-resolution encoder
features, and predicts a class for each output pixel. Training commonly
uses pixel-wise losses and task-specific metrics.

The sketch shows one skip connection for clarity; practical U-Nets use
several resolutions and corresponding connections.

## Practical example

A medical-imaging model can use U-Net to assign a tissue class to each
pixel. Evaluate overlap and boundary quality, and ensure image-level
splits prevent related slices from leaking across training and test sets.

## Common misconceptions

- U-Net is an architecture, not a particular pretrained model.
- Pixel-level segmentation quality can be poor even when image-level
  classification is accurate.
